paper.title: Adverse workplace conditions, high-involvement work practices and labor turnover: Evidence from Danish linked employer-employee data
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement. The title-page note states: …

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark Integrated Labour Market Database (IDA)
registers.role: sample frame for employment spells, source of the separation measure behind quit, firm characteristics (firm size, industry) and linkage of workers to establishments

registers.name_in_paper: The Danish Work Environment Cohort Study (DWECS)
registers.years: 1990-2005 (split panel collected every 5 years); the 2000 and 2005 waves are used
registers.role: treatment variables (workplace hazards, scheduling hazards, human hazards, repetitive work) and high involvement work practices (voice, information sharing, training); the 2005 wave supplies the improve outcomes
sample frame: the 2000 DWECS wave was drawn randomly from it

linkages: Within IDA, data on establishments are consistently linked to data on individuals using the unique identification numbers assigned to all establishments and individuals.
IDA is matched to DWECS at the individual level.
The 2000 DWECS wave is linked to the 2005 DWECS wave for the same individuals (the same questions on adverse workplace conditions were asked in both waves).

sample.universe: Private-sector workers in Denmark aged 18-69 interviewed in the 2000 wave of DWECS (about 6000 workers drawn randomly from the central population register, around 4500 of them in the private sector), matched to IDA
selection_rules: 2000 wave of DWECS: about 6000 workers aged 18-69 drawn randomly from the central population register
keep private-sector workers only (around 4500), because voluntary turnover cannot be defined with precision for public-sector workers
drop the 286 workers who separated involuntarily (were laid off) during 2000
listwise deletion on the variables of each specification: N ranges from 3057 in the most parsimonious specification to 2963 in the least parsimonious specification

for the five-year improvement analysis (Table 7): keep workers who faced the relevant adverse condition at the beginning of 2000 and are also observed in the 2005 wave (N = 848 physical hazards, 321 bad boss, 343 voice)

construction_notes: quit: all workers who separated during November 2000-October 2001 from the firm they were registered for as employees as of November 2000 are identified first; the self-reported primary reason for separation is then used to classify the separation as voluntary. The authors note this reason measure is subjective and probably overestimates the number of true voluntary separations.

Residual wage = actual wage minus the worker's predicted wage from an estimated standard Mincerian wage equation; it enters Eq. (1) in logs as a proxy for efficiency wage and for the wage-hazard trade-off.
All workplace hazard and HIWP variables are 0/1 indicators built from DWECS questionnaire items (Table 1).

improve is built separately for each condition: = 1 if a worker exposed to physical hazards (resp. with a bad boss) at the beginning of 2000 is no longer exposed (resp. no longer has a bad boss) in 2005; for voice, = 1 if a worker without voice in 2000 has voice in 2005.
Controls in Eq. (1): age, age squared, tenure, tenure squared, education, female, married, ln(residual wage), 6 occupation dummies, 12 industry dummies, 12 region dummies and 4 firm size categories.
Tables 4-6 use a parsimonious version of Eq. (1): night shift as the only scheduling hazard, bad boss as the only unsupportive-workplace variable, and the three conflict-at-work variables dropped.

links.pointer_quote: Using Danish linked employer–employee data, we find that: (i) exposing the worker to physical hazards leads to a 3 percentage point increase in the probability of voluntary turnover from the average rate of 18%

claims.statement: Exposure to physical hazards at work raises a private-sector worker's probability of voluntarily quitting her firm within the year.

register_source.value: DWECS (Danish Work Environment Cohort Study), 2000 wave questionnaire; no Statistics Denmark register variable is named for this item

definition.value: = 1 if the worker was exposed to: (i) noise so loud that he/she has to raise his/her voice to talk with other people; (ii) vibrations from hand tools; (iii) vibrations from strike his/her whole body; or (iv) bad lighting, 0 otherwise (Table 1).

timing.value: Self-reported in the 2000 wave of DWECS (interview in October-December 2000), i.e. at the beginning of the November 2000-October 2001 turnover window.

register_source.value: IDA (Statistics Denmark Integrated Labour Market Database) matched to DWECS; separations are taken from the register, the primary reason for separation is self-reported. No register variable name is given.

definition.value: = 1 if during the course of the year the worker separates voluntarily from the firm she was originally registered for as an employee at the beginning of the year, 0 otherwise (Table 1). Built by identifying all workers who separated during November 2000-October 2001 from the firm they were registered for as employees as of November 2000, then classifying the separation as voluntary using the self-reported primary reason for separation.

timing.value: Measured over the year November 2000-October 2001, i.e. the 12 months following the 2000 interview.

units.value: change in the probability of voluntary turnover during the year, i.e. a logit marginal effect expressed as a probability (the paper reads the Table 3 value 0.032 as '3 percentage points')

magnitude.interpretation: the 3-percentage-point increase amounts to a significant 17-percent increase in quit

estimand.time_horizon: voluntary turnover during the year following the 2000 interview (November 2000-October 2001)
estimand.formal_query: E[Quit|do(Physical hazards=1)] - E[Quit|do(Physical hazards=0)] for private-sector workers in the 2000 DWECS sample

population.description: Private-sector workers in Denmark aged 18-69 who responded to the 2000 wave of the Danish Work Environment Cohort Study and are matched to IDA, excluding the 286 workers laid off during 2000 and observations with missing values.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across workers in self-reported workplace conditions and high involvement work practices in the 2000 DWECS wave; no reform, instrument or discontinuity is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the controls of Eq. (1) (age, age2, tenure, tenure2, education, female, married, ln(residual wage), occupation, industry, region and firm size dummies), the regressor Physical hazards is independent of the unobserved determinants of voluntary turnover u.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test. The authors motivate the control set (residual wage as a proxy for efficiency wage and for the wage-hazard trade-off) and report that results are insensitive to adding union membership, collective bargaining coverage and a job satisfaction dummy.

given: ln(residual wage) (actual minus predicted wage from a Mincerian wage equation)

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample conditions on private-sector employment, on responding to the 2000 DWECS wave and on not having been laid off during 2000 (286 workers dropped); this conditioning is assumed not to distort the estimate.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 3 reports that adding the laid-off workers back 'makes little difference to the results'; no evidence is offered on survey non-response.

key_assumptions.assumption: The log-odds of quitting is linear and additive in the regressors of Eq. (1) (logit functional form).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Eq. (1) is printed; the restriction itself is not tested.

threats_discussed: the primary reason for separation is self-reported and 'probably overestimates the number of true voluntary separations'
endogeneity of wages: residual wage is included as a control but is itself endogenous and no reliable instrument is available
cost-cutting HR practices are not observed in the data and can only partly be proxied by the wage variable
multicollinearity among the three work environmental hazard variables
robustness_checks: union membership and collective bargaining coverage dummies added as extra controls - results not sensitive
a dummy for not being satisfied with the job added - results changed little
actual wage, and the worker's perception of her wage relative to effort and qualifications, used instead of residual wage - little change in the estimated marginal effects
the 286 workers laid off during 2000 added back to the sample - little difference to the results
unresolved_confounders: endogeneity of wages (the authors state that the lack of reliable instruments prevents them from accounting for it)
unobserved cost-cutting HR practices
endogeneity of job satisfaction (used only as a robustness control)

ambiguities: Significance levels are given in the running text only; Tables 3-7 print marginal effects and robust standard errors, with no stars, p-values or confidence intervals.
